candidates.title: Safety-Certified EEG Decoding via Semidefinite Programming Robustness Bounds
candidates.summary: This work adapts semidefinite programming (SDP) robustness certification to EEGNet, providing formal guarantees on classification stability under input perturbations. The method computes certified perturbation radii for motor imagery EEG signals, addressing safety concerns in clinical BCI systems. Unlike prior EEGNet evaluations, which focused on accuracy, this approach quantifies resilience to adversarial and natural signal variations.
candidates.gap: While ref-001 demonstrates EEGNet's cross-paradigm generalization, it does not provide formal robustness certification. Existing SDP-based methods (ref-005, ref-020) and Lipschitz constant estimation (ref-009, ref-022) for robustness certification have not been applied to EEGNet, leaving an open question: can these techniques be adapted to certify the safety of compact CNN architectures like EEGNet under EEG-specific signal variations?
candidates.approach: The approach applies the SDP framework from ref-005 and ref-020 to EEGNet, modeling each layer's activation functions (e.g., ELU) as quadratic constraints. Input perturbations are bounded by $\ell_2$ or $\ell_\infty$ norms. The method computes layer-wise Lipschitz constants via SDP, deriving certified robustness regions as the maximum perturbation magnitude that cannot change the classification decision. Unlike ref-005's general networks, this work incorporates EEGNet's depthwise separable convolutions into the SDP formulation to exploit temporal filtering structure.
candidates.evaluation: Evaluation uses the BCI Competition IV 2a motor imagery dataset (ref-001, ref-007), comparing certified robustness radii against CLEVER scores (ref-009) and adversarial attack success rates. Baselines include: (1) standard EEGNet (ref-001), (2) Parseval-constrained EEGNet (ref-010), and (3) PGD-adversarial-trained EEGNet (ref-013). Ablation studies isolate the SDP contribution by comparing certified radii before/after applying Lipschitz constraints. Metrics include average certified radius, CLEVER score correlation, and attack success rate reduction under $\ell_2$ and $\ell_\infty$ perturbations.

candidates.title: Cross-Paradigm Adversarial Transferability in EEG-Based BCIs: A Quantitative Analysis
candidates.summary: This work quantifies adversarial transferability across BCI paradigms (P300, MRCP, SMR) by generating universal perturbations on one paradigm and testing their effectiveness on others. The study uses EEGNet as the target model, with transferability measured via attack success rates and feature-space distance metrics, revealing paradigm-specific vulnerability patterns.
candidates.gap: While ref-021 and ref-024 study adversarial detection and UAPs in BCIs, they do not systematically analyze cross-paradigm transferability. Ref-021 evaluates detectors across datasets but does not generate cross-paradigm attacks, and ref-024 demonstrates UAP transferability within a single paradigm. The core gap is the absence of a controlled comparison between cross-paradigm and within-paradigm UAP transferability.
candidates.approach: Generate universal adversarial perturbations (UAPs) for each paradigm (P300, MRCP, SMR) using the TLM method (ref-024) on EEGNet (ref-001). For each source-target paradigm pair (e.g., P300→SMR), measure attack success rate (ASR) and compute layer-wise cosine similarity between source and target model features. The central mechanism differs from ref-024 by explicitly comparing cross-paradigm vs. within-paradigm UAPs and quantifying feature similarity as a predictor of transferability.
candidates.evaluation: Compare cross-paradigm UAP ASRs against (1) within-paradigm UAP baselines (ref-024) and (2) random noise baselines. Use MOABB (ref-007) datasets: PhysioNet P300, BNCI Horizon MRCP, and Cho SMR. Compute Spearman correlation between cosine similarity (layer 4 of EEGNet) and ASR across paradigm pairs. Ablate TLM's role by repeating experiments with fixed perturbation magnitudes.

candidates.title: Interpretable Adversarial Detection in EEG-BCIs via Spectral-Spatial Feature Disentanglement
candidates.summary: This paper proposes a Mahalanobis distance-based anomaly detection framework that disentangles spectral and spatial EEG features to improve interpretability and generalization in adversarial detection for BCIs. The method models class-conditional Gaussian distributions separately for spectral and spatial feature subspaces, enabling targeted anomaly scoring and visualization of perturbation impacts.
candidates.gap: While ref-021 demonstrates high detection AUC using Mahalanobis distance on raw feature embeddings, it does not disentangle spectral and spatial EEG characteristics, limiting interpretability of which feature dimensions are perturbed. EEGNet (ref-001) extracts both spectral and spatial features but does not isolate their contributions to adversarial detection.
candidates.approach: Extract EEGNet embeddings, decompose them into spectral (frequency band power) and spatial (electrode topography) subspaces via learned linear projections. Train separate class-conditional Gaussian models for each subspace. Compute anomaly scores as the sum of Mahalanobis distances in each subspace. Inputs: EEG trials; Outputs: Per-subspace anomaly scores; Objective: Minimize reconstruction error of spectral-spatial decomposition while maximizing detection AUC; Update rule: Alternating optimization of decomposition matrices and Gaussian parameters; Differs from ref-021: Explicit spectral-spatial disentanglement via subspace modeling.
candidates.evaluation: Test on three MOABB datasets (ref-007) used in ref-021: BNCI Horizon 2014001, PhysioNet MI, and BCIC IV IIa. Compare against ref-021's Mahalanobis detector and LID baseline under FGSM, PGD, and UAP attacks. Report AUC, true positive rate at 1% false positive rate, and ablation study isolating spectral/spatial contributions. Visualize decision boundaries via t-SNE on both subspaces to demonstrate interpretability.
